Topic: math

The mathematics behind machine learning, rebuilt from the basics: follow one prediction of a tiny language model through one training step, and meet each idea (vectors and matrices, probability, information, derivatives, optimisation, statistics) at the moment the model needs it. One training step, in one screen

About 29 minutes to read the main line (6,700 words; a little longer than most topic roots, because it starts from zero). The boxes marked "optional" add about 5 minutes, the glossary at the end can be skimmed, and the animations are extra. Every symbol is explained where it first appears and collected in the Glossary. Numbers marked illustrative are made up to show a shape; every other number is computed from the tiny model below, and the script that recomputes them is in the page's source folder.

Almost all the mathematics an ML engineer needs shows up in one training step of one model. This page follows a single prediction of a tiny language model through that step, and introduces each area of maths at the moment the step needs it, never before.

The running example: a three-word language model

The model knows three words (its vocabulary): cat, dog and sat. It has just read "the cat" and must guess the next word. The right answer is sat. A real language model does exactly this, with a vocabulary of about 100,000 pieces of words (tokens) instead of three, and with thousands of numbers per word instead of two.

  • "The cat" has been turned into a list of two numbers, x=(2,1)x = (2, 1). How a real model gets this list is the job of its earlier layers; here we simply fix it.
  • The model has one table of six numbers, WW, with one row per word: cat (1,0)(1, 0), dog (0,1)(0, 1), sat (1,−2)(1, -2). These six numbers are what training changes.
  • With these numbers the model scores the words (2,1,0)(2, 1, 0), turns the scores into probabilities (0.665,0.245,0.090)(0.665, 0.245, 0.090), and so bets on cat. It gave the right word only 9%. It is wrong, and the rest of the page is about what happens next.

The whole training step. Each box is coloured by the area of maths that enters there; the number under each box is the tiny model's actual value. Read it left to right (on a phone, top to bottom). Nothing here needs to make sense yet: each section below explains one box.

The seven steps, one lesson each

Vectors and matrices: turn the input into scoresA word is a list of numbers (a vector); a layer is a table of numbers (a matrix). Multiplying them takes one dot product per row, and each dot product measures how well the input matches that word. Probability: turn scores into a bet, and score the betSoftmax turns any scores into probabilities. The loss is minus the log of the probability given to what really happened; choose a distribution and the loss follows. Information: what the loss number meansMinus log probability is surprise, measured in bits or nats. The training loss is an average surprise (cross-entropy); it can never fall below the data's own unpredictability (entropy). Derivatives: which way to change each numberA derivative says how much the loss moves when one number moves. The chain rule multiplies local slopes; for softmax plus cross-entropy the result collapses to "prediction minus target". Optimisation: how far to stepStep against the gradient, scaled by a learning rate. Curvature sets the largest safe step: above 2 divided by the largest curvature, the steps overshoot and grow. Statistics: was the improvement real?One sentence improving proves little. Average many, and the error bar shrinks like one over the square root of how many; compare before and after on the same sentences. Reading an equation in a paperName every symbol, find every shape, read the operations inside out, plug in tiny numbers, then ask why each piece is there.
The one idea to keep
Training is a loop of four moves: score (linear algebra), bet and pay (probability and information), find the downhill direction (derivatives) and step (optimisation), followed by one question asked from outside the loop, did it really get better (statistics). When a paper or a training run confuses you, ask which of the five moves it is about.

Three tabs sit beside this one. The Notation decoder translates symbols you will meet in papers (Greek letters, subscripts, the shapes of things). The Gradient lab lets you change a tiny model's numbers and watch each step of this page recompute. Practice drills gives short exercises with worked answers, the way interview questions are asked.

1. Vectors and matrices: from an input to one score per word

The question this step raises. The model holds the input as two numbers and its knowledge as a table of six. How does it turn them into one score for each word, and why should a high score mean "likely"?

The picture

Draw the input x=(2,1)x = (2, 1) as an arrow from the origin: two steps right, one step up. Draw each word's row of WW as an arrow too. The score of a word is large when its arrow points the same way as the input arrow, zero when the two are at right angles, and negative when they point apart. Press play to watch the three scores being computed, one row at a time.

The words, then the formula

A vector is an ordered list of numbers, such as x=(2,1)x = (2, 1); how many numbers it holds is its dimension (here 2). A matrix is a table of numbers with rows and columns; its shape is written rows by columns, so WW is 3×23 \times 2. The dot product of two vectors of the same dimension multiplies them entry by entry and adds the results. Multiplying a matrix by a vector, the matrix-vector product, is one dot product per row:

z=Wx,zi=∑j=1dWijxj=wi⋅xz = W x, \qquad z_i = \sum_{j=1}^{d} W_{ij}\, x_j = w_i \cdot x
xx
the input vector, with d=2d = 2 entries x1=2x_1 = 2, x2=1x_2 = 1.
WW
the weight matrix, V×d=3×2V \times d = 3 \times 2: one row per word of the vocabulary (V=3V = 3 words).
WijW_{ij}
the number in row ii, column jj of WW. The first subscript is always the row.
wiw_i
row ii of WW, itself a vector: wcat=(1,0)w_{\text{cat}} = (1, 0), wdog=(0,1)w_{\text{dog}} = (0, 1), wsat=(1,−2)w_{\text{sat}} = (1, -2).
∑j=1d\sum_{j=1}^{d}
"add up, for jj from 1 to dd". The capital sigma is a loop written in one symbol.
zz
the output vector of scores, one per word. Raw scores like these, before they are turned into probabilities, are called logits.

In plain words: to score a word, multiply the input's numbers by that word's numbers, pair by pair, and add. Do it once per word.

The numbers
zcat=1×2+0×1=2z_{\text{cat}} = 1 \times 2 + 0 \times 1 = 2, zdog=0×2+1×1=1z_{\text{dog}} = 0 \times 2 + 1 \times 1 = 1, zsat=1×2+(−2)×1=0z_{\text{sat}} = 1 \times 2 + (-2) \times 1 = 0. So z=(2,1,0)z = (2, 1, 0): the model likes cat best.

Why a dot product measures "match"

The length (or norm) of a vector is ‖x‖=x12+x22\lVert x \rVert = \sqrt{x_1^2 + x_2^2}, Pythagoras' theorem; for the input, 4+1=2.236\sqrt{4 + 1} = 2.236. The dot product can be rewritten with lengths and the angle θ\theta between the two arrows:

w⋅x=‖w‖‖x‖cos⁡θw \cdot x = \lVert w \rVert \, \lVert x \rVert \cos\theta

where cos⁡θ\cos\theta is 1 when the arrows point the same way, 0 at a right angle and −1-1 when they point opposite ways. Dividing out the lengths leaves the cosine similarity, cos⁡θ=w⋅x‖w‖‖x‖\cos\theta = \frac{w \cdot x}{\lVert w \rVert \lVert x \rVert}. For the tiny model: cat 0.894 (nearly aligned), dog 0.447, sat 0 (exactly at right angles, so its score is 0 whatever the lengths). So a big score means "this word's arrow points where the input points, and both are long". Training will, in effect, turn the sat arrow towards the input.

Shapes: the check that catches most mistakes

A 3×23 \times 2 matrix times a 2-entry vector gives a 3-entry vector. In general an m×nm \times n matrix needs an input with nn entries and gives an output with mm: the inner sizes must match and the outer sizes survive. The transpose W⊤W^\top swaps rows and columns (2×32 \times 3 here); it appears in section 4, where the gradient runs backwards through the layer. A real model scores many inputs at once by stacking them as the columns of a matrix XX of shape d×Bd \times B (a batch of BB inputs); WXWX then has shape V×BV \times B, one column of scores per input. Writing the shape beside every symbol is the single best habit for reading papers and for debugging code.

Optional: rank, and why LoRA works (a preview)

A preview: rank, and why LoRA works

In section 5 the model will change WW by a matrix that is a column times a row: the gradient vector (0.665,0.245,−0.910)(0.665, 0.245, -0.910) times the input (2,1)(2, 1), an outer product. Every row of that change is a multiple of the same row (2,1)(2, 1). Its rank, the number of independent directions a matrix really uses, is 1. The singular value decomposition (SVD) says any matrix is a sum of such rank-1 layers, largest first, and keeping only the largest few is the best possible compression of that size (the Eckart-Young theorem). LoRA fine-tunes a large model by learning only a low-rank change BABA, with BB of shape d×rd \times r and AA of shape r×dr \times d: for d=4096d = 4096 and r=8r = 8 that is 2×4096×8=65,5362 \times 4096 \times 8 = 65{,}536 trainable numbers instead of 40962=16,777,2164096^2 = 16{,}777{,}216, or 0.39%. It works because, as the authors hypothesised and then checked experimentally, the change fine-tuning makes has a low "intrinsic rank" (LoRA, Hu et al. 2021).

What it is used for in ML
Every layer of every network is a matrix multiplication followed by something simple. Word embeddings are vectors; attention scores are dot products between a query vector and key vectors; retrieval and search rank documents by cosine similarity of embeddings; LoRA and other low-rank methods rest on rank.
Go deeper (optional): change xx and WW in the Gradient lab and watch the scores move; shapes, subscripts and transposes as papers write them are in the Notation decoder; norms, eigenvalues, the SVD worked by hand and matrix calculus: a linear algebra child page is coming. LoRA in full: LoRA (paper page) and Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT).

2. Probability: from scores to a bet, and the price of a wrong bet

The question this step raises. The scores (2,1,0)(2, 1, 0) are not probabilities: scores can be negative and need not add up to 1. How does the model turn them into a bet over the three words, and once the right word is revealed, how do we put a number on how bad the bet was?

The picture: softmax

Softmax does two things. It makes every score positive by raising the number ee to it, and then it divides by the total so the results add up to 1. Press play to watch the three bars go through both moves; then pick a temperature to see the same scores turned into a sharper or flatter bet.

The words, then the formula

A probability distribution over the vocabulary is one number per word, each between 0 and 1, adding up to 1. Picking one word with these probabilities is a draw from a categorical distribution (the many-sided version of a coin flip). Softmax builds one from any scores:

pi=ezi∑j=1Vezjp_i = \frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_{j=1}^{V} e^{z_j}}
ee
Euler's number, about 2.718. eze^{z} (the exponential, also written exp⁡(z)\exp(z)) is always positive and multiplies by 2.718 each time zz grows by 1.
ziz_i
the score (logit) of word ii, from section 1.
pip_i
the probability the model gives word ii.
VV
the vocabulary size, 3 here; the sum in the denominator runs over every word.

In plain words: exponentiate every score, then share 100% out in proportion.

The numbers
ez=(e2,e1,e0)=(7.389,2.718,1)e^{z} = (e^2, e^1, e^0) = (7.389, 2.718, 1), which add to 11.107. Dividing, p=(0.665,0.245,0.090)p = (0.665, 0.245, 0.090): cat 66.5%, dog 24.5%, sat 9.0%. Adding 10 to every score gives exactly the same pp, because every ezie^{z_i} is multiplied by the same e10e^{10}, which cancels: only differences between scores matter.

A temperature TT divides the scores first, pi∝ezi/Tp_i \propto e^{z_i / T} (the symbol ∝\propto means "proportional to": divide by the total afterwards). At T=0.5T = 0.5 the bet sharpens to (0.867,0.117,0.016)(0.867, 0.117, 0.016); at T=2T = 2 it flattens to (0.506,0.307,0.186)(0.506, 0.307, 0.186). Language models sample text this way, and contrastive models such as CLIP learn their temperature.

Scoring the bet: likelihood and the loss

The right word was sat. The likelihood of the model is the probability it gave to what actually happened: 0.090. Over many sentences that are independent (no sentence tells you anything about another), the probability of all of them is the product of each one's probability. Products of thousands of small numbers underflow to zero on a computer, so we take the logarithm, which turns products into sums: ln⁡(ab)=ln⁡a+ln⁡b\ln(ab) = \ln a + \ln b. The log of a probability is negative, so we flip the sign to get a positive number that is small when the bet was good. That is the negative log-likelihood (NLL), and it is the loss:

L=−ln⁡pyL = -\ln p_y
yy
the index of the right word (sat). Training data supplies it.
pyp_y
the probability the model gave to the right word.
ln⁡\ln
the natural logarithm, the inverse of eze^{z}: ln⁡ez=z\ln e^{z} = z, ln⁡1=0\ln 1 = 0, and ln⁡p\ln p is negative for any pp below 1.

In plain words: the loss is how much probability you failed to put on the truth, on a log scale. A perfect bet (py=1p_y = 1) costs 0; a bet that gave the truth almost nothing costs a lot, without limit.

The numbers
L=−ln⁡0.090=2.408L = -\ln 0.090 = 2.408. Had the right word been cat, the loss would have been −ln⁡0.665=0.408-\ln 0.665 = 0.408. A uniform guess, 13\frac13 each, would have cost ln⁡3=1.099\ln 3 = 1.099 whatever the answer: the model did worse on this sentence than not knowing anything.

Making the NLL as small as possible over a whole dataset is called maximum-likelihood estimation (MLE): choose the numbers that make the observed data most probable. Adding a penalty on large weights (weight decay) turns it into MAP estimation, the same thing with a prior belief that weights are small. Because this loss is a proper scoring rule (its expected value is lowest when the predicted probabilities equal the true ones), a well-trained model's probabilities can be read as probabilities, which is what calibration checks.

Choose a distribution, and the loss follows

The same move gives every standard loss: say what kind of thing the target is, pick the distribution that describes it, and take minus the log of its probability.

TargetDistributionIts NLL is calledLoss for one exampleTiny example
yes or noBernoulli: 1 with probability ppbinary cross-entropy (BCE)−[yln⁡p+(1−y)ln⁡(1−p)]-[y \ln p + (1 - y)\ln(1 - p)]spam filter says 0.8; spam: 0.223, not spam: 1.609
one of VV classescategoricalcross-entropy−ln⁡py-\ln p_ythe tiny model: 2.408
a real numberGaussian with fixed width σ\sigmasquared error (MSE)(y−μ)22σ2+const\frac{(y - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2} + \text{const}σ=1\sigma = 1, predict 2.5, truth 3: 0.125 + 0.919

Here yy is the observed target (0 or 1 for the Bernoulli), pp the predicted probability of a 1, μ\mu the predicted mean and σ\sigma the assumed spread; "const" does not depend on the model, so it does not change the training. A sigmoid classifier is a Bernoulli model, which is the whole relation between the Bernoulli distribution and binary classification. Getting the target type wrong (squared error on a yes-or-no label) is choosing the wrong distribution, not just the wrong loss.

Two meanings of "independent" (a question you flagged)

In an experiment, the independent variable is what you set (the input xx) and the dependent variable is what you measure (the target yy): "yy depends on xx".

In probability, two random quantities are independent when knowing one tells you nothing about the other: P(X,Y)=P(X)P(Y)P(X, Y) = P(X)\,P(Y), equivalently P(Y|X)=P(Y)P(Y \mid X) = P(Y), where P(Y|X)P(Y \mid X) reads "the probability of YY given XX". Learning is only possible because input and target are dependent in this sense: the next word after "the cat" is not distributed like a random word. If they were independent, the best any model could do is predict how common each word is. And the "independent" in i.i.d. (independent and identically distributed) is the probability meaning: it is what lets the likelihood of a dataset be a product.

What it is used for in ML
The softmax output layer of every classifier and language model; temperature in sampling; choosing the loss for a new target (counts, ratings, ranges); calibration and uncertainty; reading "loss plus regulariser" as likelihood plus prior.

3. Information: what the loss number means

The question this step raises. The loss is 2.408. 2.408 of what? Is that a lot? And how low could it ever go?

The picture: surprise

Before the answer was revealed, the model had a belief about each word. The rarer it thought a word, the more surprised it is to see it. The bars show how surprised the model would be by each word, in bits; the dashed line is the average surprise it expects, weighting each bar by how likely the model thinks that word is.

cat (p = 0.665)0.588 bits
dog (p = 0.245)2.031 bits
sat (p = 0.090), the truth3.473 bits
expected surprise (entropy)1.201 bits

Surprise −log2⁡p-\log_2 p of each word under the model's bet p=(0.665,0.245,0.090)p = (0.665, 0.245, 0.090); bar lengths are to scale (3.473 bits is the full width). The truth was the word the model found most surprising.

The words, then the formulas

The surprise (or information content) of an outcome you gave probability pp is −log⁡p-\log p. It is 0 for a certain event, grows as pp shrinks, and adds up over independent events (because logs turn products into sums), which is the property that forces the logarithm. With log2⁡\log_2 the unit is the bit; with the natural log ln⁡\ln it is the nat, and 1 nat is 1/ln⁡2=1.4431/\ln 2 = 1.443 bits. Training code uses ln⁡\ln, so a loss printed during training is in nats. Our loss of 2.408 nats is 2.408×1.443=3.4732.408 \times 1.443 = 3.473 bits: the model was as surprised as you would be by three and a half fair coin flips all coming up heads.

The entropy of a distribution is its average surprise (this answers a question you flagged, "what is entropy"):

H(p)=−∑ipilog⁡piH(p) = -\sum_{i} p_i \log p_i
pip_i
the probability of outcome ii; an outcome with pi=0p_i = 0 adds nothing (by convention 0log⁡0=00 \log 0 = 0).
−log⁡pi-\log p_i
the surprise of outcome ii; the sum weights each surprise by how often it happens.

In plain words: how uncertain you are before you look. A fair coin has 1 bit of entropy; a coin that lands heads 90% of the time has only 0.469 bits, because you are rarely surprised. Entropy is also the shortest possible average length of a message describing the outcome, in bits per outcome, for any lossless code (Shannon's source coding theorem): frequent outcomes get short codewords of about −log2⁡p-\log_2 p bits.

The numbers
The model's bet has entropy 0.665×0.5880.665 \times 0.588 +0.245×2.031+\, 0.245 \times 2.031 +0.090×3.473+\, 0.090 \times 3.473 =1.201= 1.201 bits (0.832 nats). A uniform bet over 3 words would have the maximum, log2⁡3=1.585\log_2 3 = 1.585 bits.

Cross-entropy is the loss; KL is the part you can remove

Now let the data come from one distribution, qq (the truth), while the model bets pp. The average surprise the model pays is the cross-entropy, and the extra it pays compared with knowing the truth is the KL divergence (Kullback-Leibler):

H(q,p)=−∑iqilog⁡pi,DKL(q‖p)=∑iqilog⁡qipi=H(q,p)−H(q)H(q, p) = -\sum_i q_i \log p_i, \qquad D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q \,\Vert\, p) = \sum_i q_i \log \frac{q_i}{p_i} = H(q, p) - H(q)
qiq_i
how often outcome ii really happens (for one training example, 1 for the right word and 0 for the rest: a one-hot vector).
pip_i
the model's probability for outcome ii.
‖\Vert
just a separator, read "from qq to pp". KL is not symmetric: DKL(q‖p)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q \Vert p) and DKL(p‖q)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p \Vert q) usually differ.

In plain words: cross-entropy is the cost of using the model's code on the real data; entropy is the cost of the perfect code; KL is the waste. KL is never negative and is 0 only when p=qp = q.

The numbers
With the one-hot target (sat), only the sat term survives: H(q,p)=−ln⁡0.090=2.408H(q, p) = -\ln 0.090 = 2.408 nats, exactly the loss of section 2. The cross-entropy loss and the negative log-likelihood are the same number. A one-hot target has entropy 0, so here all of it is KL: all of it could be removed.

On real text the target is not one-hot. After "the cat" real writers continue with "sat", "is", "was" and many more, so the data has an entropy above zero, and no model can push its average loss below the entropy of the text itself. That is why a language model's loss levels off well above 0: the part that remains is the text's own unpredictability, not a failure to learn.

Optional: which way round KL is taken (forward against reverse)

Which way round KL is taken matters. Training by cross-entropy minimises DKL(data‖model)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\text{data} \Vert \text{model}), which punishes the model hard for giving almost no probability to anything that really happens, so it spreads its bets to cover everything (mode-covering). The KL penalty used in RLHF, DKL(policy‖reference)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\text{policy} \Vert \text{reference}), is the other direction: it punishes the trained model for putting probability where the reference has little, and lets it drop some of what the reference does, which tends to narrow its outputs (mode-seeking).

Perplexity and bits per byte: the loss as a reader sees it

Perplexity is elosse^{\text{loss}} with the loss in nats per token (or 2loss2^{\text{loss}} in bits): the number of equally likely choices that would be as confusing. On our sentence it is e2.408=11.1e^{2.408} = 11.1: worse than a uniform guess over the 3 words (perplexity 3). Perplexity depends on how text is cut into tokens, so it can only be compared between models that share a tokenizer. Bits per byte divides the total surprise in bits by the length of the text in bytes, which no tokenizer can change. If our token is " sat" with its leading space (4 bytes), its 3.473 bits are 0.868 bits per byte illustrative. The Pile paper prefers bits per byte "due to its invariance to different tokenization schemes", and measures 0.29335 GPT-2 tokens per byte, so 2.0 nats per token there is 0.29335×2.0/ln⁡2=0.8460.29335 \times 2.0 / \ln 2 = 0.846 bits per byte (Gao et al. 2020).

What it is used for in ML
Reading training curves (nats per token) and language-model evaluations (perplexity within one tokenizer, bits per byte across tokenizers); the loss floor; KL penalties in RLHF and DPO; distillation (cross-entropy against a teacher's soft probabilities); entropy bonuses for exploration in RL; information gain in decision trees; mutual information and contrastive learning (see the four hats below).
Go deeper (optional): convert between nats, bits, perplexity and bits per byte in Practice drills; codes, KL in both directions with pictures, mutual information and InfoNCE: an information theory child page is coming. KL penalties in practice: Alignment: SFT, RLHF, DPO Family, RLVR and RL for LLMs.

4. Derivatives: which way to change each number

The question this step raises. The model has six numbers it may change. Which of them should go up, which down, and by how much does each one matter? Trying every change would be hopeless for a real model with billions of numbers.

The picture: a slope

Hold everything fixed except the sat score zsatz_{\text{sat}}, and draw the loss as that one score varies. The curve falls as the score rises (a higher score for the right word is better). The slope of the curve at the current point says how fast the loss falls per unit of score. Drag the score and watch the slope.

The words, then the formulas

The derivative of a function at a point is its slope there: the change in output divided by a tiny change in input,

dfda≈f(a+h)−f(a)hfor a small h\frac{df}{da} \approx \frac{f(a + h) - f(a)}{h} \quad \text{for a small } h

When a function has several inputs, the partial derivative ∂L∂zi\frac{\partial L}{\partial z_i} (the curly ∂\partial reads "partial") is the slope along one input with the others held fixed. Collecting all of them gives the gradient ∇zL\nabla_z L (read "grad of LL with respect to zz"), a vector with one slope per input, with the same shape as zz. It points in the direction that increases the loss fastest, so training moves the other way.

The numbers
Raise zsatz_{\text{sat}} from 0 to 0.1 and the loss goes from 2.408 to 2.317, a change of −0.091-0.091; divided by 0.1, the slope is about −0.91-0.91.

The chain rule: multiply local slopes

The loss does not see zsatz_{\text{sat}} directly. It sees psatp_{\text{sat}}, which depends on zsatz_{\text{sat}}. The chain rule says that the slope through a chain of steps is the product of the slopes of each step:

∂L∂zsat=∂L∂psat⋅∂psat∂zsat\frac{\partial L}{\partial z_{\text{sat}}} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial p_{\text{sat}}} \cdot \frac{\partial p_{\text{sat}}}{\partial z_{\text{sat}}}

In plain words: if the loss falls 11 units per unit of probability, and the probability rises 0.08 per unit of score, then the loss falls about 11×0.0811 \times 0.08 per unit of score.

The numbers
L=−ln⁡psatL = -\ln p_{\text{sat}} has slope −1/psat=−11.107-1/p_{\text{sat}} = -11.107. The softmax output psatp_{\text{sat}} has slope psat(1−psat)p_{\text{sat}}(1 - p_{\text{sat}}) =0.090×0.910=0.0819= 0.090 \times 0.910 = 0.0819 with respect to its own score. The product is −11.107×0.0819=−0.910-11.107 \times 0.0819 = -0.910, matching the slope measured above.

The famous result, derived without skipping a step: prediction minus target

Do this once by hand and you will never need to memorise it.

  1. Write the probability out: py=ezy∑jezjp_y = \frac{e^{z_y}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}}.
  2. Take minus the log. The log of a fraction is the log of the top minus the log of the bottom, and ln⁡ezy=zy\ln e^{z_y} = z_y: L=−ln⁡py=−zy+ln⁡∑jezjL = -\ln p_y = -z_y + \ln \sum_j e^{z_j}
  3. Differentiate the first term with respect to some score zkz_k: −zy-z_y has slope −1-1 if kk is the right word (k=yk = y) and 0 otherwise.
  4. Differentiate the second term. The slope of ln⁡u\ln u is 1/u1/u times the slope of uu (chain rule), and the only part of ∑jezj\sum_j e^{z_j} that moves with zkz_k is ezke^{z_k}, whose slope is itself: ∂∂zkln⁡∑jezj=ezk∑jezj=pk\frac{\partial}{\partial z_k} \ln \sum_j e^{z_j} = \frac{e^{z_k}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}} = p_k
  5. Add the two pieces. With yky_k meaning 1 for the right word and 0 otherwise (the one-hot target): ∂L∂zk=pk−yk,∇zL=p−y\frac{\partial L}{\partial z_k} = p_k - y_k, \qquad \nabla_z L = p - y

In plain words: push each score down by the probability the model gave it, and push the right word's score up by 1. The gradient is the prediction minus the target.

The numbers
∇zL=(0.665,0.245,0.090)−(0,0,1)\nabla_z L = (0.665, 0.245, 0.090) - (0, 0, 1) =(0.665,0.245,−0.910)= (0.665, 0.245, -0.910). The entries add up to 0 (adding the same amount to every score changes nothing, section 2). A finite-difference check, nudging each score by ±0.001\pm 0.001, gives (0.6652,0.2447,−0.9100)(0.6652, 0.2447, -0.9100).
The same collapse for every standard loss (a question you flagged: differentiating each cost function)

Binary cross-entropy on a sigmoid output p=σ(z)=1/(1+e−z)p = \sigma(z) = 1/(1 + e^{-z}): ∂L/∂p=p−yp(1−p)\partial L/\partial p = \frac{p - y}{p(1 - p)} and σ′(z)=p(1−p)\sigma'(z) = p(1 - p), so their product is ∂L/∂z=p−y\partial L/\partial z = p - y. Squared error (yˆ−y)2(\hat{y} - y)^2 on an identity output: 2(yˆ−y)2(\hat{y} - y) (times 1/n1/n for a mean over nn examples). All three are prediction minus target, because each pairs a distribution with its natural output function (sigmoid for Bernoulli, softmax for categorical, identity for Gaussian). Pair them wrongly, for example squared error on a sigmoid, and an extra factor p(1−p)p(1 - p) remains, which goes to 0 when the model is confidently wrong: at z=−6z = -6 with y=1y = 1, cross-entropy's slope is −0.9975-0.9975 but squared error's is −0.0049-0.0049, about 200 times smaller, so learning stalls exactly when it is most needed.

From the scores back to the weights: backpropagation

Each score is zi=∑jWijxjz_i = \sum_j W_{ij} x_j, so nudging the weight WijW_{ij} moves ziz_i by xjx_j per unit. By the chain rule, ∂L/∂Wij=gixj\partial L/\partial W_{ij} = g_i\, x_j, where g=∇zLg = \nabla_z L. For the whole matrix, and for the input:

∇WL=gx⊤,∇xL=W⊤g\nabla_W L = g\, x^\top, \qquad \nabla_x L = W^\top g
gx⊤g\, x^\top
a column (3 entries) times a row (2 entries): a 3×23 \times 2 matrix, the same shape as WW. Every gradient has the shape of the thing it is the gradient of.
W⊤gW^\top g
the transpose sends the 3 slopes back to the 2 inputs: what an earlier layer would receive.
The numbers
∇WL\nabla_W L has rows cat (1.330,0.665)(1.330, 0.665), dog (0.489,0.245)(0.489, 0.245), sat (−1.820,−0.910)(-1.820, -0.910): each row is gig_i times (2,1)(2, 1), so it has rank 1, as promised in section 1. ∇xL=(−0.245,2.065)\nabla_x L = (-0.245, 2.065).
Optional: what backpropagation costs, and why memory runs out first

Backpropagation is the chain rule run from the loss backwards, one layer at a time. Each layer receives the gradient with respect to its output, a vector vv, and passes back the gradient with respect to its input, v⊤Jv^\top J, where JJ is the layer's Jacobian (the table of every output's slope with respect to every input). This vector-Jacobian product is computed directly (here W⊤gW^\top g), never by building JJ, which for a real layer would be enormous. Notice the cost: the forward pass did one matrix product (WxWx); the backward pass does two (gx⊤g x^\top for the weights and W⊤gW^\top g for the input). That is why a backward pass costs about twice a forward pass, and why training costs about 6 floating-point operations per parameter (embeddings aside) per token, 2 forward and 4 backward (Kaplan et al. 2020, section 2.1). It also needs the forward pass's inputs (xx here) to be kept in memory until the backward pass uses them, which is why memory, not arithmetic, usually runs out first; activation checkpointing stores only some of them and recomputes the rest, training an nn-layer network in memory proportional to n\sqrt{n} for the cost of one extra forward pass (Chen et al. 2016).

What it is used for in ML
Every training run (autograd frameworks run exactly this); checking a hand-written gradient with finite differences; diagnosing vanishing or exploding gradients; numerical stability (frameworks fuse softmax and cross-entropy so the gradient never divides by a tiny probability); memory planning for large models.
Go deeper (optional): the Gradient lab shows every gradient of this model live and checks it by finite differences; the symbols ∂\partial, ∇\nabla and ⊤\top and the two layout conventions for derivatives are in the Notation decoder; derive the sigmoid and MSE gradients in Practice drills; Jacobians, Hessian-vector products and forward against reverse mode: a calculus and optimisation child page is coming. Memory at scale: Distributed Training.

5. Optimisation: how far to step

The question this step raises. The gradient says which way is downhill. How far should the model move? A tiny step wastes time; a huge one might jump over the valley and land higher than it started.

The picture: one step, before and after

The model moves every weight a little against its gradient. Press play to watch one step of the tiny model: the gradient, the new weights, the new scores and the new bet, with the loss falling. Then choose a bigger step size and run it again.

The words, then the formula

Gradient descent replaces every weight by itself minus a small multiple of its slope:

W←W−η∇WLW \leftarrow W - \eta\, \nabla_W L
←\leftarrow
"replace with": the left side takes the value computed on the right.
η\eta
the learning rate (Greek "eta"), the step size, a positive number you choose.
∇WL\nabla_W L
the gradient from section 4, the same shape as WW.

In plain words: move each number a little in the direction that lowers the loss, in proportion to how much it matters.

The numbers
With η=0.1\eta = 0.1 the rows become cat (0.867,−0.067)(0.867, -0.067), dog (−0.049,0.976)(-0.049, 0.976), sat (1.182,−1.909)(1.182, -1.909). The new scores are (1.667,0.878,0.455)(1.667, 0.878, 0.455), the bet (0.571,0.259,0.170)(0.571, 0.259, 0.170) and the loss 1.773, down from 2.408. A shortcut shows why: the new scores are W′x=Wx−ηgx⊤xW'x = Wx - \eta\, g\, x^\top x =z−η‖x‖2g= z - \eta \lVert x \rVert^2 g, and ‖x‖2=5\lVert x \rVert^2 = 5, so each score moves by −0.5-0.5 times its gradient. With η=0.3\eta = 0.3 one step already flips the bet to sat (0.459, loss 0.778); with η=1\eta = 1 the loss drops to 0.011. Repeating η=0.1\eta = 0.1 for 20 steps brings it to 0.083.

Curvature: why too big a step blows up

The slope changes as you move; how fast it changes is the curvature, the second derivative. Take the simplest bowl, L(θ)=12λθ2L(\theta) = \frac12 \lambda \theta^2, whose slope is λθ\lambda\theta and whose curvature is the constant λ\lambda (Greek "lambda"). One gradient step gives

θ←θ−ηλθ=(1−ηλ)θ\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta \lambda \theta = (1 - \eta\lambda)\,\theta

so each step multiplies the distance from the bottom by 1−ηλ1 - \eta\lambda. That shrinks the distance only if |1−ηλ|<1|1 - \eta\lambda| < 1, that is if 0<η<2/λ0 < \eta < 2/\lambda. Between 1/λ1/\lambda and 2/λ2/\lambda the steps overshoot to the other side but still shrink; above 2/λ2/\lambda every step lands further away than the last. Watch both sides of the line:

With many weights, the curvature is a matrix, the Hessian HH, holding the second derivative for every pair of weights. Its eigenvalues are the curvatures along its principal directions, the directions in which the bowl is a simple parabola. Gradient descent stays stable only if η<2/λmax⁡\eta < 2/\lambda_{\max}, with λmax⁡\lambda_{\max} the largest eigenvalue: the steepest direction sets the limit for all of them. The condition number κ=λmax⁡/λmin⁡\kappa = \lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min} says how lopsided the bowl is. Because the step must be small enough for the steepest direction, the flattest one creeps: for curvatures 1 and 10 (κ=10\kappa = 10) the limit is η=0.2\eta = 0.2, the best fixed step 2/11=0.1822/11 = 0.182 shrinks the error only to 9/11=0.8189/11 = 0.818 of itself per step, and cutting it a thousandfold takes 35 steps. That long narrow valley is the picture behind most slow training.

The numbers for the tiny model
For softmax cross-entropy the Hessian with respect to the scores is diag⁡(p)−pp⊤\operatorname{diag}(p) - p\,p^\top (a matrix with pi(1−pi)p_i(1 - p_i) on the diagonal and −pipj-p_i p_j elsewhere). At p=(0.665,0.245,0.090)p = (0.665, 0.245, 0.090) its eigenvalues are 0, 0.119 and 0.371. With respect to WW each is multiplied by ‖x‖2=5\lVert x \rVert^2 = 5, so λmax⁡=1.855\lambda_{\max} = 1.855 and the local limit is η≈2/1.855=1.08\eta \approx 2/1.855 = 1.08. The step with η=1\eta = 1 was just inside it. The limit moves as training goes: as the bet grows confident, p(1−p)p(1 - p) shrinks and the bowl flattens.
Optional: what practical optimisers (Newton, Adam, normalisation) do about curvature, and convexity

What practical optimisers do about it (intuition only). Newton's method divides the gradient by the curvature, −H−1g-H^{-1} g, so every direction gets the right step at once; for a billion weights HH has 101810^{18} entries, so it is out of reach, but boosted trees use it: each XGBoost leaf takes the Newton step −G/(H+λ)-G/(H + \lambda) from its summed gradients and curvatures (this λ\lambda is a regularisation strength, not an eigenvalue). Adam gives each weight its own step size, dividing by the square root of an exponential moving average of that weight's squared gradients; its authors relate that average to the diagonal of the Fisher information, a curvature-like quantity met again below, but it is not a Newton step (Kingma and Ba 2014). Normalisation layers and careful initialisation make the bowl rounder (a smaller κ\kappa). In full-batch training of real networks, the top curvature tends to rise until it sits just above 2/η2/\eta, and training still progresses at that "edge of stability" (Cohen et al. 2021).

The softmax cross-entropy loss is convex in the scores (its Hessian has no negative eigenvalues: every chord lies above the curve, so any minimum is the global one). A deep network's loss in its weights is not, and in high dimensions most points where the gradient is zero are saddles rather than minima (Dauphin et al. 2014).

What it is used for in ML
Choosing and scheduling learning rates (warmup exists partly because curvature is high early); diagnosing a loss that oscillates and then explodes right after the learning rate was raised; why Adam, momentum, normalisation and good initialisation help; second-order methods (Newton, L-BFGS, K-FAC, XGBoost's leaves).
Go deeper (optional): run many steps and push the learning rate past the limit in the Gradient lab; momentum, Adam, Muon and schedules: Optimisers and learning-rate schedulers; conditioning in practice: Normalisation and initialisation; the Hessian, Newton, convexity and Lagrange multipliers in depth: a calculus and optimisation child page is coming.

6. Statistics: was the improvement real?

The question this step raises. On "the cat" the loss fell from 2.408 to 1.773. That was guaranteed: the step was computed from this very sentence. The real question is whether the model got better at text it has not seen, and one sentence cannot tell you.

The picture: one noisy measurement against the average of many

Score the model before and after the step on held-out sentences (text kept aside, never trained on), and record, for each sentence, how much its loss changed. Some sentences improve, some get worse; the changes scatter. Below, each dot is one sentence's change, the thick line is the running average and the band is its 95% interval. With one sentence the band is so wide it says nothing; as sentences accumulate it narrows. illustrative The changes are simulated: drawn at random around a true average of −0.1-0.1 nats with a spread of 0.5.

The words, then the formula

The mean of nn measurements is their average. Their standard deviation ss is their typical distance from the mean (the square root of the average squared distance, the variance). The mean is itself uncertain, and its uncertainty, the standard error, shrinks with the square root of nn:

d‾=1n∑i=1ndi,SE=sn,95% interval: d‾±1.96SE\bar{d} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} d_i, \qquad \mathrm{SE} = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}, \qquad \text{95\% interval: } \bar{d} \pm 1.96\,\mathrm{SE}
did_i
the change in loss on sentence ii (after minus before; negative means better).
d‾\bar{d}
the mean change (the bar means "average").
ss
the standard deviation of the individual changes.
1.96
for a bell-shaped (normal) spread, 95% of the probability lies within 1.96 standard deviations of the centre.

In plain words: averaging nn noisy numbers divides the noise by n\sqrt{n}. Four times as much data halves the error bar; a hundred times as much divides it by ten.

The numbers
With a spread of s=0.5s = 0.5 nats per sentence, the standard error is 0.5 for one sentence, 0.25 for 4, 0.125 for 16, 0.05 for 100 and 0.025 for 400. A true improvement of 0.1 nats is about as big as the 95% half-width at 100 sentences (1.96×0.05=0.0981.96 \times 0.05 = 0.098), so around 100 is where it starts to show; at 400 it is clear. For an accuracy near 50% on 500 questions, each answer is a 0-or-1 with spread 0.5×0.5=0.5\sqrt{0.5 \times 0.5} = 0.5, so the standard error is 0.25/500=0.022\sqrt{0.25/500} = 0.022 and the 95% interval is about ±4.4\pm 4.4 points: a 1-point gain on a 500-question benchmark is invisible.

Why 1.96 works even though one sentence's change is not bell-shaped: the central limit theorem says the average of many independent measurements is approximately normal whatever the shape of each one, with standard deviation s/ns/\sqrt{n}.

Compare on the same sentences. Sentences differ wildly in difficulty: a model's loss might range over several nats from one sentence to the next, while the before-and-after change on each sentence varies far less illustrative. Subtracting per sentence (a paired comparison) cancels the shared difficulty, which is why the dots above are per-sentence changes rather than two separate averages. Comparing two unpaired averages would carry all the difficulty noise twice and need far more sentences for the same certainty.

Optional: the same square root inside training (minibatch noise)

The same n\sqrt{n} runs through training itself: a minibatch gradient is the average of the gradients of BB examples, a noisy estimate of the full-data gradient whose noise shrinks like 1/B1/\sqrt{B}. That noise is why stochastic gradient descent wobbles, and part of why it escapes saddles.

What it is used for in ML
Error bars on benchmark scores and on the difference between two checkpoints; deciding how many evaluation examples you need; A/B tests; variance across random seeds; batch size and gradient noise; refusing to believe a one-point gain on a small evaluation set.
Go deeper (optional): paired tests, McNemar's test, the paired bootstrap and how many items an evaluation needs are worked through on Eval statistics: error bars, paired tests, how many items you need (this page does not repeat them); compute error bars yourself in Practice drills; p-values, concentration inequalities and bias against variance: a probability and statistics child page is coming.

The same object in different hats

Two objects turn up in several of the sections above under different names. Seeing that they are one thing each is the payoff of learning the areas together.

Cross-entropy wears four hats

The old version of this page used a set of scores read four ways; here it is again, checked. Take the same scores z=(2,1,0)z = (2, 1, 0) and probabilities p=(0.665,0.245,0.090)p = (0.665, 0.245, 0.090), but suppose the right word had been cat (the model's favourite) rather than sat.

Probability: a likelihood

Model the next word as a categorical draw. The negative log-likelihood of cat is −ln⁡0.665=0.408-\ln 0.665 = 0.408 nats; minimising its average over a dataset is maximum-likelihood estimation (section 2).

Information: a code length

Divided by ln⁡2\ln 2, the same number is 0.588 bits: the length of cat's codeword in a code built from the model's bet. Averaged over real data it is the cross-entropy, the data's entropy plus the KL divergence from the data to the model (section 3).

Calculus: prediction minus target

Its gradient with respect to the scores is p−y=(0.665−1,0.245,0.090)p - y = (0.665 - 1, 0.245, 0.090) =(−0.335,0.245,0.090)= (-0.335, 0.245, 0.090), adding up to 0 (section 4).

Contrastive learning: InfoNCE

Read cat as an anchor's matching partner (the positive) and dog and sat as two non-matching candidates, with similarity scores 2, 1 and 0. Then 0.408 is the InfoNCE loss with N=3N = 3 candidates, and it certifies that the two views share at least ln⁡3−0.408=0.691\ln 3 - 0.408 = 0.691 nats of mutual information (how much knowing one tells you about the other), by the bound I≥ln⁡N−LI \ge \ln N - L (van den Oord et al. 2018).

With the real answer, sat, the same reading gives a loss of 2.408, and the bound ln⁡3−2.408\ln 3 - 2.408 is negative: it certifies nothing. The bound can never exceed ln⁡N\ln N, which is why contrastive models such as CLIP train with huge batches (32,768 pairs, so N−1N - 1 negatives for each positive; Radford et al. 2021).

Curvature is read three ways

For a yes-or-no prediction with score zz and probability p=σ(z)p = \sigma(z), three quantities from three different areas turn out to be the same number, p(1−p)p(1 - p):

Optimisation: the Hessian

The second derivative of the binary cross-entropy loss with respect to zz is p(1−p)p(1 - p), whatever the label yy.

Statistics: a variance

A Bernoulli label that is 1 with probability pp has variance p(1−p)p(1 - p).

Probability: the Fisher information

The score (the slope of the log-likelihood with respect to zz) is y−py - p; its variance, the Fisher information, is p(1−p)p(1 - p).
The numbers (checked)
At z=0z = 0 (p=0.5p = 0.5) all three are 0.25, their largest value. At z=ln⁡9=2.197z = \ln 9 = 2.197 (p=0.9p = 0.9) all three are 0.09. A confident prediction sits in a flat part of the loss. The tiny model shows the many-word version: the Hessian of its loss with respect to the scores, diag⁡(p)−pp⊤\operatorname{diag}(p) - p\,p^\top, is exactly the covariance matrix of the one-hot draw, whose diagonal holds the per-word variances pi(1−pi)=(0.223,0.185,0.082)p_i(1 - p_i) = (0.223, 0.185, 0.082) (a simulation of 200,000 draws gives 0.222, 0.185, 0.081), and it is the Fisher information of the categorical distribution in its scores. The ratio of its largest to smallest nonzero eigenvalue is the condition number of section 5.
Optional: why this matters for natural gradients, and a correction to the old page

Because, for these matched pairs (sigmoid with BCE, softmax with cross-entropy, identity with squared error), the curvature with respect to the scores does not depend on the label, it equals its own average over labels, the Fisher. That is why natural-gradient methods and K-FAC precondition with the Fisher, and why the curvature of TRPO's KL constraint is the Fisher matrix. A correction to the old page: this equality is exact with respect to the scores only. With respect to the weights of a deep network the Hessian gains an extra term (the residual p−yp - y times the curvature of the network itself), so there the Fisher equals the Hessian only approximately; it is exactly the "generalised Gauss-Newton" part of it (Martens 2020, New insights and perspectives on the natural gradient method).

Which area to reach for is a diagnosis
Cannot see why a loss is that loss and not another: probability (choose the distribution and the loss is decided). A run has run out of memory and you cannot see where it went: calculus, and nearly always the backward pass's stored activations. A representation has collapsed, or a fine-tune has barely moved anything: linear algebra, and the word is rank. An evaluation number will not say what it means: information theory. A claimed gain might be noise: statistics. The loss oscillates and explodes after a learning-rate change: optimisation, and the word is curvature.

How to read an equation in a paper

An equation in a paper is a compressed paragraph. Expanding it takes five steps, always in the same order. Here they are on the most-cited equation in modern ML, scaled dot-product attention, equation 1 of Attention Is All You Need (Vaswani et al. 2017):

Attention⁡(Q,K,V)=softmax⁡(QK⊤dk)V\operatorname{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{Q K^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) V
  1. Name every symbol. QQ holds the queries (one row per position asking "what should I look at?"), KK the keys (one row per position, "what I contain"), VV the values (one row per position, "what I hand over"), dkd_k the length of each query and key row, ⊤\top the transpose (section 1), softmax as in section 2, applied to each row separately. If a symbol is not defined near the equation, search the paper for its first use; the Notation decoder lists the conventions papers assume without saying.
  2. Write the shape beside every symbol. With nn queries and mm keys: QQ is n×dkn \times d_k, KK is m×dkm \times d_k, so K⊤K^\top is dk×md_k \times m and QK⊤QK^\top is n×mn \times m: one score for every query-key pair. Softmax keeps that shape; VV is m×dvm \times d_v, so the result is n×dvn \times d_v, one output row per query. If the shapes do not fit, you have misread a symbol.
  3. Read the operations from the inside out, in words. Take the dot product of each query with each key (how well they match, section 1); divide by dk\sqrt{d_k}; turn each query's row of scores into weights that add up to 1 (softmax); and return, for each query, the weighted average of the value rows.
  4. Plug in tiny numbers. Reuse the tiny model: one query q=x=(2,1)q = x = (2, 1), the three keys are the rows of WW, and dk=2d_k = 2. The raw scores are (2,1,0)(2, 1, 0) as in section 1; divided by 2\sqrt{2} they are (1.414,0.707,0)(1.414, 0.707, 0), and softmax turns them into weights (0.576,0.284,0.140)(0.576, 0.284, 0.140). If the values are also the rows of WW, the output is 0.576(1,0)+0.284(0,1)0.576\,(1, 0) + 0.284\,(0, 1) +0.140(1,−2)+\, 0.140\,(1, -2) =(0.716,0.004)= (0.716, 0.004): mostly cat's row, a little of the others. Without the division the weights would be (0.665,0.245,0.090)(0.665, 0.245, 0.090), sharper.
  5. Ask why each piece is there. Why dk\sqrt{d_k}? The paper's footnote: if the entries of a query and a key are independent with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has variance dkd_k. With dk=64d_k = 64 raw scores would typically be about 8 apart, softmax would put nearly all the weight on one key, and its gradients would vanish (section 4); dividing by dk\sqrt{d_k} brings the variance back to 1. A term you cannot justify is usually the thing the paper is really about.
The habit
Name, shape, read, plug, ask. Ten minutes of this on a paper's central equation saves an hour of rereading prose around it, and step 4 is also how you test your own derivations: if tiny numbers do not come out right, the algebra is wrong.
Go deeper (optional): the Notation decoder translates the symbols and conventions papers use; the paper itself, with a live toy Transformer: Attention Is All You Need (paper page); practise the five steps on other equations in Practice drills.

Glossary

Every term and symbol introduced on this tab, in the order the training step meets them. Each name links to the place it is explained.

Terms

Vocabulary: the set of tokens a language model can output (3 words here, about 100,000 in real models).
Vector: an ordered list of numbers; its dimension is how many.
Matrix: a table of numbers; its shape is rows by columns.
Dot product: multiply two vectors entry by entry and add; large when they point the same way.
Matrix-vector product: one dot product per row of the matrix.
Weight matrix: the numbers a layer learns.
Logits: raw scores before softmax.
Length (norm): ‖x‖=∑ixi2\lVert x \rVert = \sqrt{\sum_i x_i^2}.
Cosine similarity: the dot product divided by both lengths; 1 aligned, 0 at right angles.
Transpose: rows and columns swapped, W⊤W^\top.
Batch: several inputs processed together as one matrix.
Outer product: a column times a row, giving a rank-1 matrix.
Rank: how many independent directions a matrix really uses.
Singular value decomposition (SVD): any matrix as a sum of rank-1 layers, largest first.
LoRA: fine-tuning by learning only a low-rank change BABA.
Probability distribution: non-negative numbers, one per outcome, adding up to 1.
Categorical distribution: one draw among several outcomes.
Softmax: exponentiate the scores, then divide by their total.
Exponential: eze^z, always positive; e≈2.718e \approx 2.718.
Temperature: divide the scores by TT before softmax; low sharpens, high flattens.
Likelihood: the probability the model gave to what actually happened.
Independent (i.i.d.): knowing one tells nothing about another; identically distributed means drawn from the same distribution.
Negative log-likelihood (NLL): −ln⁡py-\ln p_y, the loss.
Maximum-likelihood estimation (MLE): choose the weights that make the data most probable.
MAP estimation: MLE plus a prior; "loss plus regulariser".
Proper scoring rule: a loss whose expected value is lowest at the true probabilities.
Bernoulli: a yes-or-no outcome; its NLL is binary cross-entropy.
Gaussian: the bell curve; its NLL is squared error.
Surprise: −log⁡p-\log p of an outcome.
Bit and nat: units of surprise with log2⁡\log_2 and ln⁡\ln; 1 nat = 1.443 bits.
Entropy: average surprise; the shortest average code length.
Cross-entropy: average surprise when the data comes from qq and you bet pp; the training loss.
KL divergence: cross-entropy minus entropy; the removable part of the loss; not symmetric.
One-hot: a vector with 1 for the right answer and 0 elsewhere.
Perplexity: elosse^{\text{loss}}; an effective number of choices; tokenizer-dependent.
Bits per byte: total surprise in bits divided by text length in bytes; tokenizer-free.
Derivative: a slope, change in output per tiny change in input.
Partial derivative: the slope along one input with the others fixed.
Gradient: all partial derivatives together; points uphill.
Chain rule: the slope through a chain of steps is the product of their slopes.
Backpropagation: the chain rule run from the loss backwards through every layer.
Jacobian: the table of every output's slope with respect to every input.
Vector-Jacobian product: what each layer computes in backprop, without building its Jacobian.
Gradient descent: W←W−η∇WLW \leftarrow W - \eta \nabla_W L.
Learning rate: the step size η\eta.
Curvature or second derivative: how fast the slope changes.
Hessian: the matrix of second derivatives.
Eigenvalues: here, the curvatures along the Hessian's principal directions.
Condition number: largest over smallest curvature; how lopsided the bowl is.
Newton's method: divide the gradient by the curvature, −H−1g-H^{-1}g.
Adam: a per-weight step size from a moving average of squared gradients.
Convex: bowl-shaped everywhere; any minimum is the global one.
Mean, standard deviation, variance: the average, the typical distance from it, and that distance squared.
Standard error: the uncertainty of a mean, s/ns/\sqrt{n}.
Central limit theorem: averages of many independent measurements are approximately normal.
Paired comparison: compare two models example by example so shared difficulty cancels.
Minibatch gradient: the average gradient over BB examples; noise shrinks like 1/B1/\sqrt{B}.
InfoNCE: cross-entropy over one positive and N−1N - 1 negatives; contrastive learning's loss.
Mutual information: how much knowing one variable tells you about another.
Score (statistics): the slope of the log-likelihood.
Fisher information: the variance of the score; the expected curvature of the NLL.

Symbols

xx, WW, zz: the input vector, the weight matrix, the scores z=Wxz = Wx.
WijW_{ij}, wiw_i: the entry in row ii, column jj; row ii.
∑j=1d\sum_{j=1}^{d}: add up over jj from 1 to dd.
‖x‖\lVert x \rVert: the length of xx.
⊤\top: transpose.
pp, pip_i, yy: the model's probabilities; the probability of word ii; the right answer (an index, or a one-hot vector).
ee, ln⁡\ln, log2⁡\log_2: Euler's number; the natural log; the base-2 log.
∝\propto: proportional to.
LL: the loss.
P(Y|X)P(Y \mid X): the probability of YY given XX.
H(p)H(p), H(q,p)H(q, p), DKL(q‖p)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q \Vert p): entropy, cross-entropy, KL divergence.
∂\partial, ∇\nabla: partial derivative; gradient (∇WL\nabla_W L: gradient of LL with respect to WW).
σ(z)\sigma(z): the sigmoid 1/(1+e−z)1/(1 + e^{-z}). (Elsewhere σ\sigma can mean a standard deviation; context decides.)
η\eta, ←\leftarrow: the learning rate; "replace with".
λ\lambda, λmax⁡\lambda_{\max}, κ\kappa: a curvature (eigenvalue), the largest one, the condition number.
HH, gg: the Hessian and the gradient (in section 3, HH is entropy: papers reuse letters).
d‾\bar{d}, ss, nn, SE\mathrm{SE}: a mean, a standard deviation, a sample size, a standard error.
QQ, KK, VV, dkd_k: attention's queries, keys, values and key length.

Fourteen equations that carry modern ML, quoted exactly as their papers print them, decoded symbol by symbol. The aim is to read the next paper's maths without getting stuck: every symbol named, every shape given with real sizes, every equation run once on tiny numbers.

How to read any equation: the five steps from the Reading tab ("How to read an equation in a paper"), used on every card
  1. Name every symbol. Find the line where the paper defines it; the same letter means different things in different papers (β\beta is a decay rate in Adam, a KL weight in DPO, a noise level in DDPM). Here: tap a symbol.
  2. Write the shape beside every symbol. Check that every product's inner sizes match; most misreadings fail this test.
  3. Read the operations from the inside out, in words. Here: the "Read it aloud" sentence.
  4. Plug in tiny numbers. Two or three tokens, a 3 by 3 matrix: compute it once by hand. Here: "With tiny numbers".
  5. Ask why each piece is there. Why the square root, why the hat, why this subscript under the E. Here: "Traps".

Each card links the paper (arXiv id, version, equation number and PDF page) and the knowledge base pages that teach the mechanism. Every worked number is recomputed by src/notation/recompute.py; numbers marked illustrative are made-up inputs run through the real formula.

Architecture

Scaled dot-product attention

Vaswani et al. 2017, Attention Is All You Need · arXiv 1706.03762v7 · Eq. (1), PDF page 4 · §3.2.1
Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax(QKTdk)V\mathrm{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\mathrm{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^{T}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}\right)V
As printed, with the paper's capital T for the transpose. The paper prints the softmax argument in plain round brackets.

Tap a symbol

Tap any symbol in the equation (the shaded parts; a wide equation scrolls sideways) or a chip above: its name, meaning, shape with concrete sizes, and where the paper defines it.
QQ: queries
Meaning
One row per position that is asking a question: what am I looking for?
Shape
n×dkn \times d_k: here 3×43 \times 4 (3 tokens, dk=4d_k = 4); in the paper's base model dk=64d_k = 64.
Defined
§3.2.1, p. 4: queries "packed together into a matrix Q".
KK: keys
Meaning
One row per position that can be looked at: what do I contain, as a label to match against?
Shape
m×dkm \times d_k: here 3×43 \times 4. Self-attention has m=nm = n; cross-attention can differ.
Defined
§3.2.1, p. 4.
T{}^{T}: transpose
Meaning
Swap rows and columns, so QKTQK^T is every query dotted with every key. Other papers write K⊤K^\top or K′K': same thing.
Shape
KTK^T is dk×md_k \times m: here 4×34 \times 3.
Defined
Not defined in the paper: standard notation.
VV: values
Meaning
One row per position: what that position hands over if you attend to it.
Shape
m×dvm \times d_v: here 3×23 \times 2; paper base dv=64d_v = 64.
Defined
§3.2.1, p. 4.
dkd_k: key dimension
Meaning
Length of each query and key vector. Dividing by dk\sqrt{d_k} keeps the dot products from growing with dkd_k (footnote 4: if the components are independent with mean 0 and variance 1, q⋅kq \cdot k has variance dkd_k).
Shape
A number: here 4, so dk=2\sqrt{d_k} = 2; paper base 64, so 8.
Defined
§3.2.1 and footnote 4, p. 4; values in §3.2.2, p. 5.
softmax\mathrm{softmax}: softmax, row by row
Meaning
Turns each row of scores into weights that are positive and sum to 1: softmax(z)j=ezj/∑lezl\mathrm{softmax}(z)_j = e^{z_j} / \sum_l e^{z_l}. Applied to each row separately (one query at a time); the paper says so in words ("apply a softmax function to obtain the weights on the values").
Shape
n×mn \times m in, n×mn \times m out: here 3×33 \times 3.
Defined
§3.2.1, p. 4 (in words; the formula itself is not printed).
Attention\mathrm{Attention}: the output
Meaning
For each query, a weighted average of the value rows.
Shape
n×dvn \times d_v: here 3×23 \times 2.
Defined
Eq. (1), p. 4.

Read it aloud

Attention of Q, K, V equals: take every query dotted with every key, divide by the square root of the key length, turn each row into weights with a softmax, and use those weights to average the rows of V.

With tiny numbers

Real tiny matrices: 3 tokens, dₖ = 4, dᵥ = 2. Step through them in the animation below; the numbers are recomputed in recompute.py.

A smaller case is worked in the Reading tab, section "How to read an equation in a paper": one query against the tiny model's three keys, dk = 2, scores (2, 1, 0), weights (0.576, 0.284, 0.140). This one adds a second and third query so the whole matrix form, and every shape, shows.

All steps at once (static)
  1. Q=[101002011111]K=[101001011100]V=[100111]\begin{gathered}Q=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\\ K=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\\ V=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{gathered}

    The inputs: three queries, three keys, three values.

  2. QKT=[101002011111][101011100010]=[201032222]\begin{gathered}QK^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\\ =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 2\end{bmatrix}\end{gathered}

    Each cell is one query dotted with one key: row 1, column 1 is 1·1 + 0·0 + 1·1 + 0·0 = 2.

  3. QKT4=[100.50001.5001111]\frac{QK^{T}}{\sqrt{4}}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0.500 \\ 0 & 1.500 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}

    Divide every score by √d_k = 2.

  4. softmax(⋅)=[0.5060.1860.3070.1220.5470.3310.3330.3330.333]\mathrm{softmax}(\cdot)=\begin{bmatrix}0.506 & 0.186 & 0.307 \\ 0.122 & 0.547 & 0.331 \\ 0.333 & 0.333 & 0.333\end{bmatrix}

    Softmax each row: every row now sums to 1. Row 3 had equal scores, so its weights are equal.

  5. [0.5060.1860.3070.1220.5470.3310.3330.3330.333][100111]=[0.8140.4940.4530.8780.6670.667]\begin{gathered}\begin{bmatrix}0.506 & 0.186 & 0.307 \\ 0.122 & 0.547 & 0.331 \\ 0.333 & 0.333 & 0.333\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\\ =\begin{bmatrix}0.814 & 0.494 \\ 0.453 & 0.878 \\ 0.667 & 0.667\end{bmatrix}\end{gathered}

    Each output row is a weighted average of V's rows; shapes (3×3)(3×2) give 3×2.

Traps

  • The softmax runs along each row (over keys), never over the whole matrix and never down a column. In code: softmax(scores, dim=-1).
  • Rows are tokens. ML papers usually stack examples or positions as rows (n×dn \times d), so a layer is XWXW, not WxWx. Check which way round a paper writes it before multiplying.
  • dk\sqrt{d_k} is the square root of the key length, not of the sequence length. Without it, scores grow with dkd_k and the softmax saturates (Vaswani et al. footnote 4).
  • The decoder's mask is not in Eq. (1): §3.2.3 says it is applied by setting illegal positions to −∞-\infty before the softmax.

Architecture

Multi-head attention

Vaswani et al. 2017, Attention Is All You Need · arXiv 1706.03762v7 · unnumbered display, PDF page 5 · §3.2.2
MultiHead(Q,K,V)=Concat(head1,…,headh)WOwhere headi=Attention(QWiQ,KWiK,VWiV)\begin{aligned}\mathrm{MultiHead}(Q,K,V)&=\mathrm{Concat}(\mathrm{head}_{1},\ldots,\mathrm{head}_{h})W^{O}\\ \text{where}\ \mathrm{head}_{i}&=\mathrm{Attention}(QW_{i}^{Q},KW_{i}^{K},VW_{i}^{V})\end{aligned}
As printed in §3.2.2 (the paper sets it as two centred lines; aligned here).

Tap a symbol

Tap any symbol in the equation (the shaded parts; a wide equation scrolls sideways) or a chip above: its name, meaning, shape with concrete sizes, and where the paper defines it.
WiQW_i^Q: query projection of head i
Meaning
A learned matrix that maps each token's dmodeld_{\text{model}}-vector to that head's query. The superscript QQ is a label, not a power.
Shape
dmodel×dkd_{\text{model}} \times d_k: here 4×24 \times 2; paper 512×64512 \times 64.
Defined
§3.2.2, p. 5: "the projections are parameter matrices".
WiKW_i^K: key projection of head i
Meaning
Same idea for keys.
Shape
dmodel×dkd_{\text{model}} \times d_k: here 4×24 \times 2.
Defined
§3.2.2, p. 5.
WiVW_i^V: value projection of head i
Meaning
Same idea for values.
Shape
dmodel×dvd_{\text{model}} \times d_v: here 4×24 \times 2.
Defined
§3.2.2, p. 5.
WOW^O: output projection
Meaning
Mixes the concatenated heads back into one vector per token.
Shape
hdv×dmodelh d_v \times d_{\text{model}}: here 4×44 \times 4; paper 512×512512 \times 512.
Defined
§3.2.2, p. 5.
headi\mathrm{head}_i: head i
Meaning
One run of scaled dot-product attention (Eq. 1) on projected inputs.
Shape
n×dvn \times d_v: here 2×22 \times 2.
Defined
§3.2.2, p. 5.
hh: number of heads
Meaning
How many heads run side by side. The paper uses h=8h = 8 and dk=dv=dmodel/h=64d_k = d_v = d_{\text{model}}/h = 64.
Shape
A number: here 2.
Defined
§3.2.2, p. 5.
Concat\mathrm{Concat}: concatenate
Meaning
Place the heads' outputs side by side, column-wise, for each token.
Shape
hh blocks of n×dvn \times d_v become n×hdvn \times h d_v: here 2×42 \times 4.
Defined
§3.2.2, p. 5.
Q,K,VQ,K,V: the inputs
Meaning
In self-attention all three are the same matrix XX of token vectors (§3.2.3).
Shape
n×dmodeln \times d_{\text{model}}: here 2×42 \times 4.
Defined
§3.2.3, p. 5.

Read it aloud

Multi-head attention runs h small attentions in parallel, each on its own learned projections of Q, K and V, glues their outputs side by side and mixes them with one more matrix W O.

With tiny numbers

Two tokens, d_model = 4, h = 2 heads, d_k = d_v = 2. The projections are chosen so head 1 reads dimensions 1 and 2 and head 2 reads dimensions 3 and 4 (illustrative weights, real arithmetic).

  1. X=[10200102]W1Q=W1K=W1V=[10010000]\begin{gathered}X=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\\ W_1^{Q}=W_1^{K}=W_1^{V}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{gathered}

    Self-attention: Q = K = V = X. Head 1's projections keep the first two coordinates.

  2. XW1=[1001]XW2=[2002]\begin{gathered}XW_1=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\\ XW_2=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\end{gathered}

    Each head sees a 2 × 2 slice: shape (2×4)(4×2) = 2×2.

  3. head1=[0.6700.3300.3300.670]head2=[1.8880.1120.1121.888]\begin{gathered}\mathrm{head}_1=\begin{bmatrix}0.670 & 0.330 \\ 0.330 & 0.670\end{bmatrix}\\ \mathrm{head}_2=\begin{bmatrix}1.888 & 0.112 \\ 0.112 & 1.888\end{bmatrix}\end{gathered}

    Eq. (1) inside each head, with √d_k = √2.

  4. Concat=[0.6700.3301.8880.1120.3300.6700.1121.888]\mathrm{Concat}=\begin{bmatrix}0.670 & 0.330 & 1.888 & 0.112 \\ 0.330 & 0.670 & 0.112 & 1.888\end{bmatrix}

    Side by side: 2 × (2+2) = 2 × 4.

  5. WO=[0.50000.500000.50000.5000.50000.500000.50000.500]ConcatWO=[1.2790.2211.2790.2210.2211.2790.2211.279]\begin{gathered}W^{O}=\begin{bmatrix}0.500 & 0 & 0.500 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.500 & 0 & 0.500 \\ 0.500 & 0 & 0.500 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.500 & 0 & 0.500\end{bmatrix}\\ \mathrm{Concat}\,W^{O}=\begin{bmatrix}1.279 & 0.221 & 1.279 & 0.221 \\ 0.221 & 1.279 & 0.221 & 1.279\end{bmatrix}\end{gathered}

    W O mixes heads: each output column takes half of one head's column and half of the other's.

Traps

  • Superscripts Q,K,V,OQ, K, V, O on WW are names, not powers; the subscript ii is the head index. WiQW_i^Q reads "W, head i, for queries".
  • hh here is the number of heads; in the LayerNorm and many RNN papers hh is a hidden state. Same letter, different object: always check the paper's own definition.
  • Splitting into heads costs no extra compute: with dk=dmodel/hd_k = d_{\text{model}}/h the paper notes the total cost is similar to one full-width head (§3.2.2).

Layer normalisation

Ba, Kiros and Hinton 2016, Layer Normalization · arXiv 1607.06450v1 · Eq. (4), PDF page 3 · §4 (μ and σ as in Eq. (3), p. 2)
𝐡t=f[𝐠σt⊙(𝐚t−μt)+𝐛]μt=1H∑i=1Haitσt=1H∑i=1H(ait−μt)2\begin{gathered}\mathbf{h}^{t}=f\left[\frac{\mathbf{g}}{\sigma^{t}}\odot\left(\mathbf{a}^{t}-\mu^{t}\right)+\mathbf{b}\right]\\ \mu^{t}=\frac{1}{H}\sum_{i=1}^{H}a_{i}^{t}\qquad\sigma^{t}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{H}\sum_{i=1}^{H}\left(a_{i}^{t}-\mu^{t}\right)^{2}}\end{gathered}
As printed (the recurrent form, superscript t is the time step), with the paper's three side-by-side parts stacked here for width. Bold marks vectors.

Tap a symbol

Tap any symbol in the equation (the shaded parts; a wide equation scrolls sideways) or a chip above: its name, meaning, shape with concrete sizes, and where the paper defines it.
𝐚t\mathbf{a}^t: summed inputs
Meaning
The vector being normalised: one layer's pre-activations for one example at time step tt. Bold means a vector; aita_i^t (not bold, subscript ii) is its ii-th entry.
Shape
HH numbers: here H=4H = 4.
Defined
§4, p. 3: "a^t = W_hh h^(t-1) + W_xh x^t".
aita_i^t: one entry of a
Meaning
The i-th hidden unit's summed input.
Shape
A number.
Defined
Eq. (3)-(4).
μt\mu^t: mean over the layer
Meaning
Average of the H entries of this one example. Not a batch mean: that is batch normalisation, Eq. (2).
Shape
A number per example (per time step).
Defined
Eq. (3), p. 2; Eq. (4), p. 3.
σt\sigma^t: standard deviation over the layer
Meaning
Square root of the average squared distance from μt\mu^t. Divides by HH, not H−1H-1: the population (biased) version.
Shape
A number per example.
Defined
Eq. (3), p. 2.
𝐠\mathbf{g}: gain
Meaning
Learned per-unit scale (modern code calls it γ\gamma or weight).
Shape
HH numbers: same dimension as 𝐡t\mathbf{h}^t.
Defined
§4, p. 3: "b and g are defined as the bias and gain parameters".
𝐛\mathbf{b}: bias
Meaning
Learned per-unit shift (modern code: β\beta or bias).
Shape
HH numbers.
Defined
§4, p. 3.
⊙\odot: element-wise product
Meaning
Multiply entry by entry (the Hadamard product), not a matrix product.
Shape
Two vectors of length H give one of length H.
Defined
§4, p. 3: "element-wise multiplication between two vectors".
ff: nonlinearity
Meaning
The activation function applied after normalising (the paper's RNN setting). In a Transformer's LayerNorm there is no f: take it as the identity.
Shape
A function, applied entry by entry.
Defined
Eq. (1), p. 2.
HH: number of hidden units
Meaning
How many entries are averaged.
Shape
A number: here 4.
Defined
Eq. (3), p. 2: "H denotes the number of hidden units in a layer".
𝐡t\mathbf{h}^t: output
Meaning
The normalised, rescaled, shifted vector.
Shape
HH numbers.
Defined
Eq. (4), p. 3.

Read it aloud

h at time t equals f of: g over sigma, times element by element the vector a minus its mean, plus b; where mu is the average of a's H entries and sigma the square root of their average squared deviation.

With tiny numbers

One example, H = 4, f = identity (as in a Transformer). Gain and bias are illustrative.

  1. 𝐚=[2468]μ=14(2+4+6+8)=5\begin{gathered}\mathbf{a}=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 & 6 & 8\end{bmatrix}\\ \mu=\tfrac14(2+4+6+8)=5\end{gathered}

    The mean of this one example's four entries.

  2. σ=14((−3)2+(−1)2+12+32)=5=2.236\begin{gathered}\sigma=\sqrt{\tfrac14\left((-3)^2+(-1)^2+1^2+3^2\right)}\\ =\sqrt{5}=2.236\end{gathered}

    Divide by H = 4, not 3.

  3. 𝐚−μσ=[−1.34−0.450.451.34]\frac{\mathbf{a}-\mu}{\sigma}=\begin{bmatrix}-1.34 & -0.45 & 0.45 & 1.34\end{bmatrix}

    Now mean 0 and (population) standard deviation 1.

  4. 𝐠=[10.50012]𝐛=[0010]𝐠⊙𝐚−μσ+𝐛=[−1.342−0.2241.4472.683]\begin{gathered}\mathbf{g}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0.500 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\\ \mathbf{b}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\\ \mathbf{g}\odot\frac{\mathbf{a}-\mu}{\sigma}+\mathbf{b}\\ =\begin{bmatrix}-1.342 & -0.224 & 1.447 & 2.683\end{bmatrix}\end{gathered}

    Scale entry by entry, then shift.

  5. with H−1: σ=20/3=2.582first entry −1.162 instead of −1.342\begin{gathered}\text{with } H-1:\ \sigma=\sqrt{20/3}=2.582\\ \text{first entry } -1.162 \text{ instead of } -1.342\end{gathered}

    The trap: dividing by H − 1 gives different outputs. PyTorch's LayerNorm uses the paper's 1/H (biased) version.

Traps

  • Bold 𝐚\mathbf{a} is the vector; plain aia_i is one entry; the superscript tt is a time step, not a power. σt\sigma^t is "sigma at time t", not sigma to the t.
  • The paper's σ\sigma has no ϵ\epsilon. Code adds one inside the square root: PyTorch's LayerNorm computes (x−E[x])/Var[x]+ϵ(x - \mathrm{E}[x])/\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}[x] + \epsilon} with ϵ=10−5\epsilon = 10^{-5} by default and the biased variance (docs).
  • The averages run over the features of one example (the layer), not over the batch. Eq. (2), batch normalisation, averages over examples with 𝔼𝐱∼P(𝐱)\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}\sim P(\mathbf{x})}.

Training

The language-modelling objective (next-token log-likelihood)

Radford et al. 2018, Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training (GPT-1) · Eq. (1), PDF page 3 · §3.1 · Not on arXiv; OpenAI's PDF.
L1(𝒰)=∑ilog⁡P(ui|ui−k,…,ui−1;Θ)L_{1}(\mathcal{U})=\sum_{i}\log P(u_{i}\mid u_{i-k},\ldots,u_{i-1};\Theta)
As printed in §3.1.

Tap a symbol

Tap any symbol in the equation (the shaded parts; a wide equation scrolls sideways) or a chip above: its name, meaning, shape with concrete sizes, and where the paper defines it.
L1L_1: the objective (to maximise)
Meaning
Total log-likelihood of the corpus. It is a sum of logs of probabilities, so it is negative and the paper maximises it. The loss you see in code is its negative, divided by the number of tokens.
Shape
A number.
Defined
Eq. (1), p. 3: "maximize the following likelihood".
𝒰\mathcal{U}: the corpus
Meaning
An unlabelled sequence of tokens {u1,…,un}\{u_1, \ldots, u_n\}.
Shape
nn token ids.
Defined
§3.1, p. 3.
uiu_i: the token to predict
Meaning
Token number ii; the sum index ii runs over positions in the corpus.
Shape
One token id (an integer in the vocabulary).
Defined
§3.1, p. 3.
ui−k,…,ui−1u_{i-k},\ldots,u_{i-1}: the context
Meaning
The kk tokens before position ii; kk is the context window (512 in GPT-1, §4.1).
Shape
kk token ids.
Defined
§3.1, p. 3: "k is the size of the context window".
PP: the model's probability
Meaning
Probability the network assigns to the actual next token. Eq. (2) says how: P(u)=softmax(hnWeT)P(u) = \mathrm{softmax}(h_n W_e^T), a softmax over the vocabulary.
Shape
A number in (0, 1], read off a vector of length |V||V| (vocabulary size).
Defined
Eq. (2), p. 3.
|\mid: given
Meaning
Conditional probability: probability of the left side given the right side.
Shape
Notation.
Defined
Standard.
;Θ;\Theta: parameters (after a semicolon)
Meaning
The semicolon separates what we condition on (data) from the parameters that define the model. It is not conditioning in the probabilistic sense.
Shape
All the network's weights (a 12-layer decoder, §4.1).
Defined
§3.1, p. 3: "neural network with parameters Θ".
log⁡\log: natural log
Meaning
Base e, as almost everywhere in ML papers; values are in nats. Divide by ln 2 for bits.
Shape
Function.
Defined
Not stated in the paper (convention).

Read it aloud

L one of U equals the sum, over every position i, of the log of the probability the model with parameters Theta gives to token u i, given the k tokens before it.

With tiny numbers

Vocabulary (the, cat, sat); corpus "the cat sat"; the model's logits at each position are illustrative, the arithmetic is real. Same logits z = (2, 1, 0) as the Reading tab's running example.

  1. P(⋅|the)=softmax(2,1,0)=[0.6650.2450.090]⇒P(cat|the)=0.245\begin{gathered}P(\cdot\mid\text{the})=\mathrm{softmax}(2,1,0)\\ =\begin{bmatrix}0.665 & 0.245 & 0.090\end{bmatrix}\\ \Rightarrow P(\text{cat}\mid\text{the})=0.245\end{gathered}

    Position 2: the right answer, cat, gets 0.245.

  2. P(⋅|the cat)=softmax(0,1,3)=[0.0420.1140.844]⇒P(sat|…)=0.844\begin{gathered}P(\cdot\mid\text{the cat})=\mathrm{softmax}(0,1,3)\\ =\begin{bmatrix}0.042 & 0.114 & 0.844\end{bmatrix}\\ \Rightarrow P(\text{sat}\mid\ldots)=0.844\end{gathered}

    Position 3: sat gets 0.844.

  3. L1=log⁡0.245+log⁡0.844=−1.408+(−0.170)=−1.577\begin{gathered}L_1=\log 0.245+\log 0.844\\ =-1.408+(-0.170)=-1.577\end{gathered}

    Sum the logs (natural log). Position 1 has no context, so it contributes nothing here.

  4. loss=−L12=0.789 nats/token=1.138 bits/tokenperplexity=e0.789=2.20\begin{gathered}\text{loss}=-\frac{L_1}{2}=0.789\ \text{nats/token}\\ =1.138\ \text{bits/token}\\ \text{perplexity}=e^{0.789}=2.20\end{gathered}

    What a training log prints: the negative, averaged per token.

Traps

  • L1L_1 is maximised; a "loss" is minimised. Papers switch between the two: check the sign and whether the text says maximise or minimise.
  • The sum is over tokens, so L1L_1 grows with corpus length; training logs report the per-token mean. Comparing a summed and a mean number is a factor of the token count.
  • log⁡\log is natural (nats). Bits per token divide by ln⁡2\ln 2; bits per byte also divide by bytes per token, and only that is comparable across tokenizers.
  • ;Θ;\Theta marks parameters, |\mid marks conditioning. Some papers write PΘ(ui|…)P_\Theta(u_i \mid \ldots) or pθp_\theta: the same thing.

Training

The Adam update

Kingma and Ba 2014, Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization · arXiv 1412.6980v9 · Algorithm 1 (the loop body), PDF page 2 · §2
gt←∇θft(θt−1)mt←β1⋅mt−1+(1−β1)⋅gtvt←β2⋅vt−1+(1−β2)⋅gt2mˆt←mt/(1−β1t)vˆt←vt/(1−β2t)θt←θt−1−α⋅mˆt/(vˆt+ϵ)\begin{aligned}g_{t}&\leftarrow\nabla_{\theta}f_{t}(\theta_{t-1})\\ m_{t}&\leftarrow\beta_{1}\cdot m_{t-1}+(1-\beta_{1})\cdot g_{t}\\ v_{t}&\leftarrow\beta_{2}\cdot v_{t-1}+(1-\beta_{2})\cdot g_{t}^{2}\\ \widehat{m}_{t}&\leftarrow m_{t}/(1-\beta_{1}^{t})\\ \widehat{v}_{t}&\leftarrow v_{t}/(1-\beta_{2}^{t})\\ \theta_{t}&\leftarrow\theta_{t-1}-\alpha\cdot\widehat{m}_{t}/(\sqrt{\widehat{v}_{t}}+\epsilon)\end{aligned}
The six update lines of Algorithm 1, as printed, without the comments in brackets.

Read it aloud

Get the gradient; update the running average of gradients and of squared gradients; correct both for starting at zero; then move each parameter by alpha times its corrected average gradient divided by the square root of its corrected average squared gradient plus epsilon.

With tiny numbers

One parameter θ, loss f(θ) = θ², so g = 2θ. Start θ0 = 1, α = 0.1 (larger than the 0.001 default so the steps are visible), β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.999, ε = 10⁻⁸.

  1. t=1: g1=2θ0=2m1=0.1⋅2=0.200v1=0.001⋅22=0.004\begin{gathered}t=1:\ g_1=2\theta_0=2\\ m_1=0.1\cdot2=0.200\\ v_1=0.001\cdot2^2=0.004\end{gathered}

    Both averages start at 0, so after one step they are far too small.

  2. mˆ1=0.2001−0.9=2vˆ1=0.0041−0.999=4\begin{gathered}\widehat{m}_1=\frac{0.200}{1-0.9}=2\\ \widehat{v}_1=\frac{0.004}{1-0.999}=4\end{gathered}

    Bias correction restores the gradient's real size.

  3. θ1=1−0.1⋅24+10−8=0.900\theta_1=1-0.1\cdot\frac{2}{\sqrt{4}+10^{-8}}=0.900

    The first step is exactly α in size, whatever the gradient's scale.

  4. t=2: g2=1.800m2=0.360v2=0.007236mˆ2=1.8947vˆ2=3.6198\begin{gathered}t=2:\ g_2=1.800\\ m_2=0.360\\ v_2=0.007236\\ \widehat{m}_2=1.8947\\ \widehat{v}_2=3.6198\end{gathered}

    Now 1 − β1² = 0.19 and 1 − β2² = 0.001999.

  5. θ2=0.900−0.1⋅1.89471.9026=0.8004\theta_2=0.900-0.1\cdot\frac{1.8947}{1.9026}=0.8004

    Again a step close to α.

  6. without the hats at t=1:0.1⋅0.2000.004=0.316\begin{gathered}\text{without the hats at } t=1:\\ 0.1\cdot\frac{0.200}{\sqrt{0.004}}=0.316\end{gathered}

    The trap: skipping bias correction makes the first step about 3 times α here.

Traps

  • Two kinds of superscript in one algorithm: gt2g_t^2 is an element-wise square, β1t\beta_1^t is a power, and tt as a subscript is a step counter.
  • The hat means "bias-corrected estimate" here. In PPO Aˆt\hat{A}_t and 𝔼ˆt\hat{\mathbb{E}}_t the hat means "estimated from samples". Same mark, related but different job.
  • ϵ\epsilon sits outside the square root in Algorithm 1. Some libraries put it inside; the difference matters only when vˆ\widehat{v} is tiny.
  • β1,β2\beta_1, \beta_2 are Adam's decay rates; the same letter β\beta is a KL strength in DPO and RLHF and a noise schedule in DDPM.

The LoRA forward pass

Hu et al. 2021, LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models · arXiv 2106.09685v2 · Eq. (3), PDF page 4 · §4.1
h=W0x+ΔWx=W0x+BAxh=W_{0}x+\Delta Wx=W_{0}x+BAx
As printed in §4.1.

Meaning
